title: Memory in the Gym
bigQuestion: How did empire, occupation and exclusion shape martial arts, and how can a school tell that history honestly on its walls?

story.title: A Photograph Above a Flag
story.kicker: A student notices that a founder's portrait hangs above a flag he never saw.
paragraphs: In a karate school in a suburb of Chicago, the front wall holds three things. In the middle is a black-and-white photograph of Funakoshi Gichin, an Okinawan teacher who brought karate to Tokyo in 1922. Below it hang two flags: the flag of the United States and the flag of Japan.

A high school student named Dana stays after class to help stack mats. She reads the small card under the photo. It says Funakoshi was born in 1868 in Shuri. That town was then the royal capital of the Ryukyu Kingdom. Japan did not take over the kingdom until 1879, when Funakoshi was a boy.

Dana asks the owner a question. "Did he ever come to America?" The owner shakes his head. Funakoshi never visited the United States. He died in Tokyo in 1957. The American flag is on the wall because the school is in America. The Japanese flag is there because the school's lineage runs through Tokyo.

Dana thinks about what is missing. There is no Ryukyu flag, no map of Okinawa, and no line about the kingdom Funakoshi was born into. She asks whether she can write a longer card for the photo. The owner says yes, if every sentence on it comes with a date and a source.
story.think: What would you put on a card under a founder's photograph so it tells the whole story honestly?

lessons.title: From Ryukyu Kingdom to Okinawa
lessons.mainIdea: Karate grew in the Ryukyu Kingdom, which Japan annexed in 1879, so its history belongs first to Okinawa and not to Japan as a whole.
reading: The *Ryukyu Kingdom* ruled the islands south of Japan from the 1400s. Its capital was Shuri, on Okinawa. The kingdom traded with China and sent tribute missions to the Chinese court. In 1609, armies from the Japanese domain of Satsuma invaded and forced the kingdom to answer to Satsuma as well.

In 1879, the Japanese government ended the kingdom. It made the islands Okinawa Prefecture and moved the last king, Shō Tai, to Tokyo. This takeover is called an *annexation*. Okinawan schools began teaching in Japanese. Local customs, dress and language came under pressure to change.

Karate grew in Shuri, Naha and Tomari, towns of the old kingdom. Teachers there drew on local practice and on ties with China. When karate reached mainland Japan in the 1920s, it arrived as an art from a recently annexed place. Historians therefore describe early karate as Okinawan, or Ryukyuan, rather than simply Japanese.

words.d: the island kingdom centered on Okinawa, ended by Japan in 1879
when one country takes over another territory and makes it part of itself
a state that rules other lands and peoples, often by force
gifts or payments a smaller state sent to a stronger one to show loyalty

lessons.title: A Hall for the Empire
lessons.mainIdea: The Dai Nippon Butokukai, founded in 1895, tied martial arts to the Japanese state until the Allied occupation dissolved it in 1946.
reading: The *Dai Nippon Butokukai*, or Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, was founded in Kyoto in 1895. That was the year Japan won its war with China. In 1899, the society opened a large hall, the Butokuden, near Heian Shrine in Kyoto. It held yearly demonstrations and awarded teaching titles.

The Butokukai grew into a national body with branches across Japan and in lands Japan ruled. It set standards for kendo, judo and other arts. In 1942, during the Second World War, the government reorganized it under state control. Its work became part of wartime training and national spirit campaigns.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, Allied officials saw the society as part of the wartime state. The Butokukai was dissolved in 1946, and many of its leaders were barred from public posts. Its story shows how a society for traditional arts could become a tool of an *empire*. Later groups used the same name, but they are separate organizations.

words.d: the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, founded in Kyoto in 1895 and dissolved in 1946
the Butokukai's demonstration hall in Kyoto, opened in 1899
to officially end an organization

check.why: The Butokukai was founded in Kyoto in 1895.

choices: They saw it as part of Japan's wartime state.
check.why: After 1945, Allied officials saw the society as part of the wartime state and dissolved it.

check.q: What happened to the Butokukai in 1942?
choices: The government reorganized it under state control.
check.why: In 1942 the government reorganized the Butokukai under state control.

lessons.title: Korea Under Colonial Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945, and many founders of the first taekwondo schools had trained in Japanese karate during those years.
reading: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it as a *colony* until 1945. Colonial schools taught in Japanese, and in the late 1930s Koreans were pressured to take Japanese names. Judo and kendo were taught in schools and police training. Many Korean students also went to Japan for university.

Several founders of the first Korean schools, the kwan, trained in karate while studying or working in Japan. Lee Won-kuk, for example, trained in Tokyo and opened Chung Do Kwan in Seoul in 1944. After liberation in 1945, these teachers built new schools. Over time, they changed names, forms and rules to make an art they saw as Korean.

Some official histories of taekwondo stress much older roots, such as Goguryeo tomb paintings and the Silla hwarang, a group of young elites. Historians agree those ancient sources exist. Many argue that modern taekwondo's direct roots run through karate learned during the colonial era. Holding both facts helps explain why the art's national story matters so much in Korea.

words.d: a land ruled by another country
Korea's freedom from Japanese rule in August 1945
a group of young elites in the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla

look.prompt: What does each poster ask you to believe? How could one wall hold both honestly?

check.why: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it until 1945.

check.why: Several founders, such as Lee Won-kuk, trained in karate while in Japan.

check.q: What do many historians argue about modern taekwondo's direct roots?

check.why: Many historians trace modern taekwondo's direct roots to karate learned during colonial rule.

lessons.title: Capoeira and the 1890 Penal Code
lessons.mainIdea: Two years after Brazil ended slavery in 1888, its 1890 penal code made capoeira a crime, and schools only became legal in the 1930s.
reading: Capoeira is an Afro-Brazilian art that grew among enslaved Africans and their descendants in Brazil. Brazil abolished slavery on May 13, 1888, with the Golden Law. It was the last country in the Americas to do so. Freed people faced poverty, police control and laws aimed at their gatherings.

In 1890, Brazil's first republican *penal code* made capoeira a crime. Its chapter on "vagrants and capoeiras" set prison terms for practicing it in streets and public squares. Police arrested practitioners for decades. The law targeted a practice linked to Black Brazilians just after emancipation.

Change came in the 1930s. In 1937, Manoel dos Reis Machado, known as Mestre Bimba, received official approval for his academy in Salvador, Bahia. In 1941, Vicente Ferreira Pastinha, known as Mestre Pastinha, opened a center for capoeira Angola. Brazil's new penal code of 1940 left capoeira out. In 2014 UNESCO listed the capoeira circle as heritage.

words.d: a set of laws that defines crimes and punishments
the legal end of slavery; in Brazil, the Golden Law of 1888
from the history and culture of Brazilians of African descent
Portuguese for master; a title for a senior capoeira teacher

check.why: Brazil abolished slavery with the Golden Law on May 13, 1888.

check.why: The 1890 code set prison terms for practicing capoeira in streets and public squares.

check.why: Manoel dos Reis Machado, Mestre Bimba, received official approval for his academy in 1937.

lessons.title: The Occupation of Japan
lessons.mainIdea: During the Allied occupation from 1945 to 1952, martial arts were removed from Japanese schools, then returned in new forms as sport.
reading: Japan surrendered in August 1945. Allied forces, led by the United States, then governed the country until 1952. This period is called the *occupation*. Occupation officials worked to remove wartime nationalism from schools, and school martial arts were stopped in late 1945.

Judo leaders argued that judo was a sport, not military training. The All Japan Judo Federation was founded in 1949, and judo returned to school programs in 1950. Kendo came back more slowly. The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, the year the occupation ended.

The return reshaped the arts as *sport*, with federations, rule books and national championships. In 1964, Tokyo hosted the Olympic Games, and judo appeared on the program for the first time. The Nippon Budokan hall was built for the judo events. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open-weight gold medal.

words.d: when a foreign power governs a country after a war; in Japan, 1945 to 1952
strong loyalty to one's nation, sometimes used to support war
a physical contest organized with rule books, federations and championships

check.why: The Allied occupation of Japan lasted from 1945 to 1952.

check.why: Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open-weight gold in 1964.

lessons.title: Judo Behind Barbed Wire
lessons.mainIdea: After 1942, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry into camps, where many kept judo and sumo clubs going.
reading: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Within days, the FBI arrested hundreds of Japanese American community leaders. Teachers of judo and kendo were among those detained, partly because their clubs had ties to groups in Japan. No evidence showed that these teachers were spies.

On February 19, 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*. It led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. About two-thirds were U.S. citizens. They were held in ten camps run by the War Relocation Authority, surrounded by barbed wire and guard towers.

Inside the camps, people built schools, churches, newspapers and sports clubs. Judo and sumo clubs met in barracks and open lots. After the camps closed, thousands of Japanese Americans moved to Chicago to start over. In 1988, the Civil Liberties Act gave a formal U.S. apology and 20,000 dollars to each surviving person who had been held. This forced removal is called *incarceration*.

words.d: the 1942 order that led to the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast
being locked up and held against one's will
the 1988 U.S. law that apologized for the camps and paid survivors

check.why: The 1988 law apologized and paid 20,000 dollars to each surviving person held.

lessons.title: Women Left Out of the Bracket
lessons.mainIdea: Women trained in judo from the 1920s, but they waited until 1980 for a world championship and until 1992 for Olympic medals.
reading: The Kodokan opened a formal women's section, the *Joshi-bu*, in 1926. Women had trained with Kanō Jigorō's support before that. For decades, though, women's judo focused on forms and training, not contests. Their ranks and titles were often limited compared with men's.

Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn, New York, entered a YMCA judo tournament in 1959. She won, but officials took her medal when they learned she was a woman. She spent the next years pushing for women's contests. In 1980, she organized the first women's world judo championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York.

Women's judo was a demonstration event at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Women first won Olympic judo medals at the 1992 Barcelona Games. Title IX, the 1972 U.S. law against sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money, helped open college and school programs. The medals on today's walls show only the years after the doors opened.

words.d: the Kodokan's women's section, formally opened in 1926
unfair treatment of people because of who they are
the 1972 U.S. law banning sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money

lessons.title: Keiko Fukuda's Long Climb
lessons.mainIdea: Keiko Fukuda began judo in 1935 and reached the highest rank only in 2011, showing how slowly rank systems opened to women.
reading: Keiko Fukuda was born in Tokyo in 1913. Her grandfather, Fukuda Hachinosuke, had taught Tenjin Shin'yō-ryū jujutsu to a young Kanō Jigorō. In 1935, Kanō invited her to train at the Kodokan's women's section. She became a teacher there and spent her life in judo.

For many years, the Kodokan limited how high women could rise in rank. Fukuda was held at fifth dan for about three decades. In 1972, after public pressure, she became one of the first two women promoted to sixth dan. She had moved to the United States in the 1960s and taught for decades in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In 2006, the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to ninth dan. In 2011, USA Judo and the U.S. Judo Federation awarded her tenth dan, the highest *rank*. She died in 2013 at age 99. Her record shows that a rank list is also a record of who was allowed to climb it, and when.

words.d: a level in a system that shows a person's standing, such as a dan grade
being raised to a higher rank
the national governing body for judo in the United States

lessons.title: A Champion Pardoned Late
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson, the first Black world heavyweight boxing champion, was convicted under a racist prosecution in 1913 and pardoned only in 2018.
reading: In the late 1800s, white heavyweight champions refused to fight Black challengers. This barrier was called the *color line*. John L. Sullivan, champion from 1882, openly drew it. Black boxers could win lesser titles but were kept from the heavyweight championship.

Jack Johnson, born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878, broke the line. On December 26, 1908, in Sydney, Australia, he beat Tommy Burns for the world heavyweight title. On July 4, 1910, in Reno, Nevada, he beat former champion James Jeffries. White mobs attacked Black Americans in many cities after that fight.

Johnson lived in Chicago and opened a nightclub there in 1912. In 1913, an all-white jury convicted him under the Mann Act, a law used against him because of his relationships with white women. He later served about a year in federal prison. In 2018, he received a posthumous *pardon*, 72 years after his death.

words.d: a barrier that kept Black athletes out of contests or titles
an official act that forgives a crime; posthumous means after death
a 1910 U.S. law that was used to prosecute Jack Johnson in 1913

look.title: Two Captions, One Photo

choices: a painted line on the ring floor

check.why: The color line was the barrier white champions used to refuse Black challengers.

check.why: Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908.

check.why: Johnson was pardoned in 2018, 72 years after his death.

lessons.title: A Founder and a Lost Games
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō won the 1940 Olympics for Tokyo, but Japan's war with China led it to give up the Games in 1938, the year he died.
reading: In 1909, Kanō Jigorō became the first Asian member of the International Olympic Committee. He led Japan's first Olympic team in 1912 in Stockholm. He worked for decades to bring the Games to Asia. In 1936, at its meeting in Berlin, the IOC awarded the 1940 Summer Olympics to Tokyo.

In July 1937, full-scale war broke out between Japan and China. Many countries questioned holding the Games in a nation at war. Kanō traveled to an IOC meeting in Cairo in 1938 to defend Tokyo's plan. On his way home, he died aboard the ship Hikawa Maru on May 4, 1938.

In July 1938, Japan's government gave up the 1940 Games. They were moved to Helsinki and then canceled because of the Second World War. Tokyo finally hosted the Olympics in 1964, with judo on the program. A fair portrait caption for Kanō can honor his work and still name the *war* that ended his Olympic plan.

words.d: the body that governs the Olympic Games
armed conflict between nations; here Japan's war with China from 1937
the short text beside a photo or object that says what it shows

look.prompt: How do these two objects connect a founder's life to a war? What would you add to the label?

choices: He was its first Asian member.

check.why: Kanō became the first Asian IOC member in 1909.

check.q: Why did Japan give up the 1940 Olympic Games in 1938?
choices: The war with China had begun.
check.why: Full-scale war with China from 1937 led Japan to give up the Games in July 1938.

check.q: Where did Kanō die in 1938?
check.why: Kanō died aboard the Hikawa Maru on May 4, 1938, returning from Cairo.

lessons.title: One Founder, Two Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Choi Hong-hi is honored in some taekwondo schools and left off the walls of others, because his life crossed a divided Korea.
reading: Choi Hong-hi was born in 1918 in the north of Korea, under Japanese rule. He studied in Japan and trained in karate there. After 1945, he became a general in the South Korean army. He founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation in Seoul in 1966 and left South Korea in 1972.

From Canada, Choi built ties with North Korea and helped bring ITF taekwondo there in the 1980s. South Korea's government regarded him as an opponent. He died in Pyongyang in 2002 and was buried there. As a result, *memory* of him differs sharply from one taekwondo school to another.

In many ITF schools, Choi's portrait hangs at the front of the room. In many schools tied to the Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo, his name rarely appears. A careful historian does not choose a side by feeling. The historian lists the dated facts, attributes each view to its group and lets readers see why the wall looks different in each room.

words.d: how a group chooses to remember and honor its past
to say clearly who holds a view or made a claim
the split into North Korea and South Korea after 1945

look.title: Two Walls, One Name
look.text: School A's front wall shows a large portrait of Choi Hong-hi with the ITF emblem. School B, a few miles away, shows the Kukkiwon building and the World Taekwondo logo, with no portrait at all. Both teach taekwondo.
look.prompt: Write two dated facts about Choi that both schools could accept. Why might each school still choose a different wall?

check.why: Choi died in Pyongyang in 2002 and was buried there.

check.q: Why is Choi honored in some schools and not in others?
choices: His life crossed a divided Korea, and groups remember him differently.
check.why: Choi's ties to both South and North Korea shape how different groups remember him.

check.q: What does it mean to attribute a view?

check.why: To attribute a view is to say clearly which person or group holds it.
